newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--March US retail sales will cap strong Q1.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--March US retail sales will cap strong Q1.

text.p: Cash tills rang up sales at a brisk pace in March, economists forecast, capping a quarter of robust U.S. consumer spending and keeping U.S. monetary authorities on alert for an overheating economy.

The Commerce Department will release its March U.S. retail sales report at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday, April 11. Economists polled by Reuters expected overall sales to have risen 0.6 percent after February's strong 0.8 percent showing. Last month, January retail sales growth was revised upward to a whopping 1.5 percent from a previous 0.6 percent gain.
Excluding automobiles, analysts forecast a 0.4 percent rise in March versus a 0.5 percent gain the prior month.

"(The March report) is going to put the cap on a very strong first quarter for consumer spending, in excess of 6 percent at an annual rate," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities.

"Also, it is going to impart positive momentum going forward into the second quarter for the consumer and keep the Federal Reserve on a heightened state of alert about the need to see some slowing in the economy," he added.
Analysts expect the March data to reflect strong sales in autos, general merchandise and apparel items, counterbalanced by reductions in building material and gasoline service station sales.

"The drop in building supply sales is primarily a weather phenomenon...while the drop in gas service stations is purely a price phenomenon," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Favorable weather for construction boosted building material sales by a large 2.2 percent in February, a rise analysts said was not repeated in March.
A slide in gasoline prices was expected to have hurt total revenues at service stations in March, analysts said.
Although March sales growth was expected to have slowed from the prior two months, analysts have seen no evidence of a near-term change in trend.
"There's no reason for suspecting that March was a clean reading of a slowdown," said Russell Sheldon, senior economist at Mellon Bank Corp.
"We will go on as before, which is that spending is too strong by a long shot but there is no evidence of inflation. It's a mystery of sorts," he added.
Moran said he looks for a natural "cooling off".
"I don't think the new equilibrium in consumer spending is five percent. We had a combination of special factors, such as good weather, tax refunds and strong job growth," he said.
"The increase in interest rates we've seen recently and the likelihood of more Fed tightening and higher interest rates will serve as a brake in the future," he added.

The Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target rate 25 basis points to 5.5 percent on March 25 at its last policysetting meeting. The next Federal Open Market Committee meeting is scheduled for May 20.
"The March report should look strong. February was too good to be true," Sheldon said.
